# Preserved Cardiorespiratory Fitness After Catheter Ablation in Athletes With Atrial Fibrillation

**Authors:** P. Nelson Hsieh; Mark É. Czeisler; Marius Chukwurah; Katie M. Stewart; Sarah K. Gustus; Kristen Steinmetz; Alexa Volfson; Conor D. Barrett; Timothy W. Churchill; Aaron L. Baggish; James S. Guseh; Eugene H. Chung

**Affiliations:** 1 Cardiovascular Performance Program, Massachusetts General Hospital, Division of Cardiology Harvard Medical School Boston MA USA | 2 Brigham and Women’s Hospital Harvard Medical School Boston MA USA | 3 RWJ Barnabas Health New Brunswick NJ USA | 4 Department of Cardiology University of Lausanne Switzerland | 5 Department of Sports Sciences University of Lausanne Switzerland

Routine exercise is generally protective against incident atrial fibrillation (AF). 1 Paradoxically, athletes engaged in large‐volume or high‐intensity endurance exercise experience higher incident AF, producing a “J‐shaped” relationship between AF risk and exercise dose. 2 , 3 Medical management for AF includes rate control and sinus rhythm maintenance. Rate control often proves challenging in athletes due to baseline bradycardia and impact on athletic performance. Pharmacologic rhythm control has undesirable drug‐specific properties (eg, use‐dependency of flecainide). Accordingly, catheter ablation has emerged as an alternative first‐line therapy for athletes with AF. 4 To date, longitudinal data examining cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) among athletes undergoing either medical maintenance of sinus rhythm or catheter ablation in athletic cohorts are limited.

We conducted a nonrandomized, retrospective, observational study examining VO2peak using cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), the gold‐standard measurement of CRF, among 51 endurance athletes with AF at a single sports cardiology center from 2013 to 2023 (Figure A). CPETs were conducted before and after catheter ablation (ablation cohort) or stabilization of medical therapy (medical cohort). This study was approved by the Massachusetts General Brigham Institutional Review Board, which waived informed consent because the analysis used deidentified clinical data. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

*Figure  : Cardiorespiratory fitness after catheter ablation in athletes. A, Athletes categorized by sport. In the cohort receiving an ablation, 53% reported EtOH use, 32% diagnosed with hypertension, and 12% had obstructive sleep apnea. In the medical therapy cohort, 56% reported EtOH use, 39% had hypertension, and 11% sleep apnea. Baseline CHA2DS2‐VASc scores and use of an anticoagulant were similar between the cohorts. Exposure to a nodal blockade agent for the ablation and medical cohorts respectively was 73% vs 56% and 61% vs 33% for antiarrhythmic drugs. All athletes received an echocardiogram. In the ablation cohort, 56% exhibited LA enlargement (>34 mL/m2 or LA AP diameter >40), compared with 55% in the medical cohort, 24% showed RA enlargement (RA medial‐lateral >25 mm/m2, superior–inferior >30 mm/m2), with 39% in the medical cohort, and 21% demonstrated RV enlargement (>41 mm basal diameter) compared with 50% in the medical cohort. B, Cardiopulmonary exercise testing procedural details and patient characteristics at time of test. Nodal blockade agents included metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol, diltiazem and verapamil. AADs included only flecainide. C, VO2peak (mL/kg per min) at index and follow‐up CPET in individual athletes with AF treated with catheter ablation or medical therapy. An exploratory multivariable linear regression model was adjusted for baseline covariates plausibly associated with both likelihood of ablation and change in exercise capacity (age, body mass index, vascular comorbidities [stroke, hypertension, coronary artery disease], alcohol use disorder, and paroxysmal vs persistent AF), physiologic predictors (baseline and ∆ resting and maximum HR), concomitant AF medications prescribed (rate control, antiarrhythmics), and interval between CPETs as a timing covariate to account for variation in follow‐up duration between tests. D, Individual athlete change in VO2peak expressed in METs for the cohort who received an ablation or medical therapy. Responders were defined as experiencing increase in VO2peak >1 MET (3.5 mL/kg per min VO2peak) after ablation and nonresponders (N=6) as experiencing decrease VO2peak >1 MET. E, Subgroup analysis of ∆VO2peak stratified by initial vs redo ablation. F, Percentage of responders (N=7) and nonresponders (N=6) after ablation stratified by baseline peak HR quartile obtained on index CPET. *Significant results as determined by P value <0.05. AAD indicates antiarrhythmic drug; AF, atrial fibrillation; AP, Anterio‐Posterior; CPET, cardiopulmonary exercise testing; DCCV, direct current cardioversion; EtOH, ethanol; HR, heart rate; LA, left atrium; MET, metabolic equivalent; RA, right atrium; and RV, right ventricle.*

The ablation and medical cohorts included 33 athletes (85% male; AF 79% paroxysmal, 21% persistent; age at index CPET 61±10 years) and 18 athletes (94% male; AF 50% persistent; age at index CPET 59±11 years), respectively. Cohorts had similar time to follow‐up CPETs (723±565 and 786±691 days, respectively). No athletes experienced stroke or withdrew from exercise activity. Time to ablation was 33.3±44.0 months after AF diagnosis; radiofrequency and cryoablation were used in 91% and 9%, respectively. Regarding lesion sets, 30% were only pulmonary vein isolation and 67% included additional lesions (eg, posterior wall).

In the ablation cohort, VO2peak was not significantly different at follow‐up compared with index CPET (mean=40±2 versus 39±2 mL/kg per min, P=0.21; Figure C and D). In contrast, VO2peak decreased significantly at follow‐up versus index CPET among athletes who received medical therapy only, who experienced an 11% relative decline (41±3 versus 36±2 mL/kg per min, P=0.01; Figure C). Subgroup analysis of the ablation cohort demonstrated no significant differences between lesion set (pulmonary vein isolation±cavotricuspid isthmus; P=0.26, pulmonary vein isolation +posterior wall isolation and additional lesions; P=0.44) and ΔVO2peak or time to AF recurrence (80% remained AF free at 1 year, P=0.88). Athletes who received de novo ablations maintained their VO2peak (41±2 versus 41±2 mL/kg per min, P=0.84). In contrast, athletes requiring redo AF ablations experienced a 9% decline in VO2peak (38±3 versus 35±3 mL/kg per min, P=0.001; Figure E).

Exploratory multivariable linear regression was performed to evaluate for the association between ablation versus medical therapy and statistically significant changes in VO2peak (ie, ∆VO2peak at follow‐up versus index CPETs). Compared with medical therapy only, catheter ablation was independently associated with significantly greater preservation of VO2peak (β=0.292 [95% CI=0.034–0.550], SE=0.127, P=0.03). In the model, which had moderate explanatory power with R2=0.44, no other covariates demonstrated statistically significant associations with the outcome (all Ps≥0.09). Given the potential effects of ablation on autonomic tone, we investigated heart rate (HR) kinetics derived from CPET pre‐ and postablation. In the ablation cohort, resting HR was significantly higher from index to follow‐up CPET (66±3 versus 69±2, P=0.01) whereas peak exercise HR showed a trend toward reduction after preablation (162±5 versus 154±3, P=0.09). Six of 7 athletes with an increase in CRF >1 metabolic equivalent after ablation fell in the top quartile of index max HR, and 4 of 6 athletes who suffered a decrease in CRF >1 metabolic equivalent fell in the bottom quartile (Figure D and F).

In sum, we report 3 principal findings. First, athletes who underwent catheter ablation showed preservation of VO2peak over 2 years (<5%), whereas those who received medical therapy experienced an 11% decrement (~5 mL/kg per min) in VO2peak; population‐based data have shown a 3.3% reduction in survival for each 1 mL/kg per min decrease in VO2peak. 5 Second, the benefit of ablation on CRF was attenuated but not eliminated in athletes requiring a repeat procedure. Whether our observations hold true with the advent of pulsed field technology remains to be seen. Finally, a preprocedural exercise test to assess max HR potentially stratified athletes by VO2peak response after ablation. Despite multivariable adjustment in the regression model, residual confounding from selection bias and unmeasured or incompletely measured variables remains possible, and observations are hypothesis generating rather than confirmatory. The modest sample size may limit precision and risk model overfitting. Our study sample was determined by an existing patient database resulting in a fixed statistical power of 93% to detect a 5% difference in follow‐up versus index VO2peak (at alpha = 0.05 and assuming an index of 40 mL/kg per min); however, some exploratory analyses may have had limited statistical power. Future randomized trials in athlete populations comparing medical therapy to ablation would address these limitations. Further, the physiological adaptations governing left atroa; remodeling and autonomic control in athletes with AF remain an active area of investigation.
